papers.title: MK-6240
papers.abstract: Flortaucipir and MK-6240 are two tau imaging agents currently in use for measuring neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) progression in Alzheimers disease (AD). The aims of this study were to use postmortem AD and Down syndrome (DS) brain sections to study three issues: (1) Measure binding affinity of flortaucipir and MK-6240 in AD brain sections by using [125I]IPPI; (2) Evaluate the binding characteristics of [18F]flortaucipir in AD, DS and cognitively normal (CN) brains sections and compare them with [18F]MK-6240, and (3) Assess the binding of [18F]flortaucipir in CN and Parkinsons disease (PD) brain sections to identify any off-target binding. The half-maximal inhibition (IC50) of [125I]IPPI bound to anterior cingulate (AC) in AD brain sections for flortaucipir was 2.91 nM and MK-6240 was 5.99 nM. Using frontal cortex (FCX) and temporal cortex (TCX) of AD, DS and CN brain sections, [18F]flortaucipir displayed high levels of binding in the gray matter (GM) of AD and DS. The average ratio of DSAD GM to CN GM was 15.7 in FCX, while DSAD GM to CN GM was 15.2 for the TCX. In the case of AD, average ratio of AD GM to CN GM was 12.4 in FCX, while AD GM to CN GM was 9.5 for the TCX. Binding of [18F]flortaucipir in brain section of AC from CN and PD cases did not exhibit any off-target binding to monoamine oxidase-A (MAO-A). In summary, both flortaucipir and MK-6240 exhibit similar high affinity to tau and [18F]flortaucipir exhibits higher binding compared to [18F]MK-6240 in DSAD.

papers.title: Automated, high-throughput kinematic analysis of skilled reaching in rodent models of neurological injury
papers.abstract: Neurological dysfunction can diminish quality of life by disrupting the movement capacity required to accomplish tasks. Kinematic studies guide treatment development by revealing subtle relationships between patterns of movement and neurological dysfunction. However, these studies produce a large quantity of opaque, multifaceted, and often highly correlated data. Here we present a novel and efficient approach to collecting, analyzing, and interpreting kinematic data with high throughput. We automated a single pellet reaching task in mice and created a video analysis pipeline that scores task success and extracts kinematic features from reaches. To analyze the resulting data, principal component analysis was first applied to group covarying measurements into a few overarching dimensions of behavior. Regularized regression was then applied separately to select reach qualities that best predicted task success. Applied to four nervous system injury models, this approach revealed differences in the effects of injury type and rehabilitative intervention on movement patterns that were not apparent from task success alone.

papers.title: Brain Signal Variability and Brain-Behavior Coupling in Adults with Dyslexia
papers.abstract: Background: Brain signal variability indexed by fMRI has emerged as a promising transdiagnostic biomarker for neurodevelopmental disorders, demonstrating better predictive utility than time-averaged metrics for diagnosis, yet it remains underexplored in adult dyslexia. The Neural Noise Hypothesis of dyslexia proposes that genetic risk disrupts cortical excitation/inhibition balance, elevating neural noise and affecting processes essential for reading. Here, we examine resting-state fMRI BOLD variability, a metric linked to neural noise, in adults with dyslexia and investigate its links with behavior. Methods: In 30 adults with dyslexia (DY) and 76 typical readers (TR), we computed three complementary BOLD variability metrics: standard deviation (SD) and mean squared successive differences (MSSD) to quantify BOLD amplitude fluctuations, and dynamic regional homogeneity (dReHo) to quantify local temporal coordination. Voxel-wise group comparisons and partial least squares correlation analyses examined brain-behavior associations across a comprehensive behavioral battery spanning reading (e.g., word reading, phonological processing), math, oral language, working memory, and executive function domains. Results: DY showed higher SD and MSSD in the left ventral occipitotemporal pathway and higher MSSD in the cerebellum, whereas TR showed higher dReHo in frontal and temporoparietal regions. SD/MSSD in visual, somatomotor, cerebellar, and subcortical networks significantly covaried with multi-domain behavioral profiles. Conclusions: Adults with dyslexia showed localized, metric-specific differences in brain signal variability and brain-behavior covariance, indicating region-specific rather than global alterations. These results suggest that brain signal variability is a promising candidate task-free phenotype that could potentially index target engagement in interventions for adult dyslexia.

papers.title: Electrophysiological dynamics of empathy for self- and other-related pain
papers.abstract: Empathy requires the ability to generate shared representations of the self and others while maintaining a distinction between them. However, it remains unclear whether, and to what extent, the neural processes involved in sharing and understanding others' pain overlap with those involved in processing one's own pain, particularly with respect to their temporal dynamics. Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying empathic processing of self- and other-related painful facial expressions. To this end, EEG signals were recorded from 42 female participants while they viewed self- and other-related painful and neutral expressions. During the early stage of processing, the difference in N2 amplitude between self-related and other-related stimuli was smaller in the painful than in the neutral condition. Nevertheless, self-related painful stimuli continued to elicit more negative N2 amplitudes and greater Alpha/Mu suppression than other-related painful stimuli. In contrast, during the late stage of empathic processing, no distinction was observed between self- and other-related painful stimuli. Instead, painful expressions, regardless of whether they were self- or other-related, elicited larger late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes. These findings suggest that empathic processing is characterized by an early self-other distinction followed by a later convergence in the neural representation of self- and other-related pain.

papers.title: Delayed Reduction in Painful Sensations Evoked by Cervical tSCS Following High-Frequency Stimulation
papers.abstract: Objective: Transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) is a non-invasive neuromodulation technique with potential effects on pain perception. However, tSCS itself can evoke discomfort or pain at higher current intensities, and it remains unclear whether high-frequency tSCS alters the pain evoked by subsequent low-frequency stimulation. This study examined whether high-frequency cervical tSCS delivered at motor-threshold intensity is followed by changes in pain ratings elicited by low-frequency tSCS in healthy participants. Approach: Twenty-five healthy participants completed a single experimental session. Individual sensory, motor, and pain thresholds were determined using single-pulse tSCS at the C6-C7 spinal level. Pain was assessed using 1-Hz stimulation delivered for 1 min at an individually defined intensity corresponding to 6-7 points on a 0-10 Numerical Rating Scale. Participants then received 80-Hz tSCS for 10 min at motor-threshold intensity, followed by three repeated pain-assessment sessions separated by 5-min intervals. Surface electromyography was recorded from the flexor carpi radialis and extensor carpi radialis. Pain analysis included 25 participants, whereas EMG analysis included 18 participants. Main results: Pain ratings were significantly lower than baseline during the second and third post-stimulation assessments. In contrast, ratings obtained immediately after high-frequency stimulation did not differ significantly from baseline. EMG responses showed substantial inter-participant variability. No EMG metric showed a significant omnibus session effect after correction for multiple comparisons, although exploratory comparisons indicated transient increases in ECR AUC and mean rectified amplitude immediately after high-frequency stimulation. Significance: These findings indicate that high-frequency cervical tSCS can exert a measurable short-term influence on pain perception. Pain ratings and stimulation-evoked EMG responses showed different temporal patterns and represent complementary, non-equivalent outcomes of spinal stimulation.

papers.title: Age and Sex Differences in Lateral Ventricle Choroid Plexus Volume in a Large, Manually Segmented, Multi-Site MRI Dataset
papers.abstract: Introduction The choroid plexus (ChP), which produces cerebrospinal fluid and forms the blood-CSF barrier, has drawn growing interest in psychiatric and neurodegenerative neuroimaging. However, prior volumetric studies have relied largely on automated segmentation tools such as FreeSurfer, which show poor agreement with manual tracing, and have been limited to small, narrow-age, single-site samples. Methods We present DataPlex, a manually segmented lateral ventricle ChP dataset comprising 700 3T T1-weighted MRI scans drawn from 35 study/site categories, spanning a wide range of age, sex, and scanner manufacturer (GE, Philips, Siemens). Using generalized least squares models accounting for within-site dependence, we examined associations between ChP and lateral ventricle (LV) volume, and age, sex, scanner manufacturer, image resolution, a registration-based quality-control metric, intracranial volume, and cognitive performance. Results ChP volume displayed a positive linear association with age and was significantly greater in males than females, while LV volume showed a significant nonlinear relationship with age and no sex difference. Scanner manufacturer and image resolution were significantly associated with measured left LV volume but not with ChP volume, and the quality-control metric was not significantly associated with any outcome. Both ChP and LV volume were significantly associated with several cognitive domains, including emotion recognition, working memory, inhibitory control, and episodic memory. Conclusion These findings demonstrate meaningful differences in ChP volume across age and sex. DataPlex represents the largest demographically and technically diverse manually segmented ChP dataset to date, establishing reference benchmarks for future automated segmentation tools and underscoring the importance of accounting for demographic and technical covariates in choroid plexus research.

papers.title: Scaling up naturalistic narrative research: A reproducible large language model-based tool for evaluating contextual information gain
papers.abstract: Narratives are a universal part of natural human experience. As experimental stimuli, narratives allow scientists to study complex mental processes with direct relevance to everyday experience. These analyses typically require manual labeling of key event features. Such characterization of narrative stimuli are extremely labor-intensive and prone to subjectivity. Automated tools could reduce these difficulties and enable scaling to longer, varied stimuli by exposing the exact quantities computed. We address this by introducing a metric that uses open-weight LLMs to compute contextual information gain. Our metric correlates with human ratings of event importance and causal centrality, critically distinguishing the latter from semantic centrality, thus overcoming limitations of existing automated tools. The metric similarly captures shared coactivation in the default mode network, a network implicated in narrative comprehension. Taken together, these results validate an automated, empirically-grounded tool that researchers can use to identify behaviorally- and neurally-relevant computational quantities in naturalistic stimuli.

papers.title: Age-associated skeletal muscle dysfunction with spinal cord pathology in an App knock-in model of Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Skeletal muscle dysfunction is increasingly recognized in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but its pathological basis remains poorly understood. We examined age-associated muscle dysfunction together with skeletal muscle and spinal motor system alterations in male AppNL-G-F/NL-G-F knock-in (App-KI) mice, which develop age-dependent amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) pathology without amyloid precursor protein (APP) overexpression. Middle-aged, but not adult, App-KI mice showed lower strength-related performance than age-matched wild-type mice, whereas skeletal muscle mass and myofiber cross-sectional area were preserved. General motor performance was also preserved, suggesting that the strength-related impairment did not simply reflect generalized motor dysfunction. Middle-aged App-KI mice had higher percentages of centrally nucleated fibers in the gastrocnemius and quadriceps femoris muscles. Transcriptomic and targeted expression analyses further revealed alterations in molecular profiles related to muscle development and myosin, including reduced expression of factors involved in myoblast fusion and selected myosin proteins. Despite evident cerebral A{beta} pathology, no apparent A{beta} immunoreactivity was detected in skeletal muscle. In the lumbar ventral horn, App-KI mice had fewer choline acetyltransferase-positive motor neurons, greater A{beta} deposition, and increased immunoreactivity for glial fibrillary acidic protein and ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1; serum interleukin-6 levels were also selectively elevated in middle-aged App-KI mice. Together, these findings indicate that age-associated reductions in strength-related performance in App-KI mice occur without overt muscle atrophy and are accompanied by histological and molecular abnormalities in skeletal muscle and pathological changes in the lumbar spinal cord. Thus, AD-related physical dysfunction may involve abnormalities in both peripheral skeletal muscle and the spinal motor system.

papers.title: Elucidating the Sodium Channel-Targeting Anti-Seizure Medication Interactome: A Drug-Target Pathway Analysis
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is a common neurological disorder in both children and adults, primarily managed with anti-seizure medications (ASMs). Sodium channel blockers are among the most commonly used ASMs. These medications exhibit distinct spectra of efficacy and side effect profiles. These likely result from different off-target interactions, protein binding profiles, and subunit selectivity that remain poorly characterized. We developed a neural network-based computational pipeline to systematically elucidate the molecular targets and associated biological pathways of selected sodium channel-modulating ASMs: carbamazepine, lamotrigine, eslicarbazepine, licarbazepine, lacosamide, phenytoin, and cenobamate. Using the DRIFT (Drug-target identification based on chemical similarity) algorithm for proteome-wide target prediction, we identified protein targets for these ASMs. The sodium channel alpha subunit family was the highest-ranked target for every drug except cenobamate, for which it ranked second behind the GABA-A receptor. Pathway mapping in the Reactome database revealed both shared and drug-specific biological processes. Furthermore, molecular docking studies elucidated the atomistic interactions between the drugs and the predicted targets. Specifically, the predicted target landscape varied from eslicarbazepine and licarbazepine (59 predicted targets each) to lacosamide (18). Pathway analysis revealed recurrent enrichment in rapid depolarisation and the interaction between L1 and ankyrins shared across all drugs, alongside predicted off-targets, including the cannabinoid CB1 receptor for phenytoin and the carbonic anhydrases for lacosamide. Molecular docking supported these predictions, with binding scores ranging from -24 to -31 kcal/mol. Overall, this work provides a systems-level view of NaV-targeting ASM pharmacology and a hypothesis-generating framework to prioritize mechanistic and combination studies of these medications in epilepsy.

papers.title: Aging enteric neurons develop chromatin remodeling, DNA damage and a senescence-like phenotype
papers.abstract: Aging is associated with gastrointestinal dysfunction, yet the cellular and molecular changes underlying aging of the enteric nervous system (ENS), the cellular network that controls gut motility and digestion, remain poorly characterized. Here, we investigated whether enteric neurons show canonical hallmarks of aging in mice and humans. We assessed age-related changes in enteric neurons of the jejunum and colon in mice aged 2, 13-15, and 22-24 months using immunofluorescence, transmission electron microscopy, calcium imaging, and network morphology analysis, and compared selected markers between young and aged human gut tissue. Enteric neurons accumulated DNA damage with age in both the jejunum and colon, with nitrergic neurons exhibiting a greater burden of damage than cholinergic neurons. Increased H3K9me3-DAPI colocalization, consistent with senescence-associated heterochromatin foci, was already seen at 15 months in both regions, revealing a potentially early driver of age-related gut changes. At 24 months, colonic neuron numbers decreased, while average neuronal soma size was increased and approximately 25-30% of neurons expressed cytoplasmic p21, a marker of senescence. Aged neurons showed enlarged, less circular mitochondria and increased pPDH immunoreactivity, indicative of declining neuronal activity. Consistent with remodeling of myenteric plexus architecture, neuronal calcium responses increased upon electrical stimulation while decreasing after agonist application. DSS-induced colitis did not reproduce the DNA damage, heterochromatin, or p21 changes seen with age, implying a direct role in the latter. Human aged enteric neurons showed higher {gamma}H2AX and H3K9me3 intensities. These data demonstrate that enteric neurons develop a senescence-like phenotype with age, and identify neuronal senescence as an underexplored aspect of ENS aging.

papers.title: Dance experience shapes local brain dynamics and shared responses during naturalistic action observation
papers.abstract: Skilled action observation unfolds over time: viewers follow changing movements, coordinate what they see with prior experience, and form a response to the performance as a whole. Dance expertise is known to alter action-related activation and the similarity of spectators' responses, but its association with local BOLD dynamics during an extended performance remains unclear. We reanalyzed fMRI from 14 professional dancers and 11 novices watching the same 33-minute dance film; one choreographer provided a separate reference. In the first 678 volumes, we measured voxelwise brain entropy (BEN) using sample entropy before summarizing it in Schaefer 400 parcels and seven networks, calculated windowed entropy from parcel-mean signals, and examined intersubject correlation (ISC) and four group-blind coactivation patterns (CAPs). After adjustment for local gray-matter volume, age, sex, and motion, dancers had higher static BEN in 32 parcels and six networks (FDR q < .05). Dynamic BEN was higher in control and default-mode networks. Dancer-dancer ISC exceeded novice-novice ISC in five networks. Dancers occupied one common CAP less often and another more often, while performer synchrony and acceleration tracked state occurrence across spectators. These converging observations show that dance experience is expressed in local temporal irregularity, shared spectator responses, and the distribution of brain states during naturalistic action observation.

papers.title: In silico designed small molecule targets misfolded TDP-43 to rescue function and ALS pathology
papers.abstract: The DNA/RNA binding protein TARDBP or TDP-43 is a key driver of pathology in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), a motor neuron disease with no known cure. In >97% of sporadic ALS patients, nuclear TDP-43 in motor neurons mislocalizes and aggregates in the cellular cytoplasm (gain-of-function). A parallel reduction in nuclear TDP-43 in ALS patients leads to a loss-of-function in mRNA binding and splicing regulation. Using our machine learning platform, we discovered ACE-339, a novel, orally bioavailable small molecule that disrupts insoluble TDP-43 aggregates. Using in vitro, in vivo and in silico models, we show that ACE-339 directly targets aggregated forms of TDP-43. ACE-339 interacts directly with TDP-43 hexamers, disaggregates recombinant TDP-43 and rescues both gain- and loss-of-function phenotypes of TDP-43 in cells. ACE-339 functionally rescues TDP-43 dependent mis-splicing and synaptic activity. Lastly, ACE-339 rescues disease associated phenotypes in two independent mouse models of TDP-43 pathology. In addition, we now have a catalog of TDP-43 disaggregating compounds that are being developed further to be tested in clinical trials in patients with ALS and other TDP-43 proteinopathies.

papers.title: Near-threshold somatosensory perception revisited: Pre- and post-stimulus neural processes during electrical and naturalistic mechanical stimulation
papers.abstract: Near-threshold somatosensory stimulation is traditionally applied to investigate the post-stimulus neural correlates of conscious perception as well as ongoing brain activity like alpha oscillations that precede stimulation and modulate perception. Recent findings showed that applying more natural mechanical stimulation instead of the frequently used electric stimulation reveals differences in early post-stimulus perceptual correlates. The precise role of pre-stimulus alpha oscillations requires deeper investigation in the electrical modality and is yet fully undiscovered in the mechanical modality. In this study we investigate post-stimulus neural correlates of conscious perception and shine light on how pre-stimulus alpha amplitude and phase coherence relate to electrical and mechanical stimulus perception. Contrary to previous findings, we found no differences between modalities in early perceptual correlates. Both modalities showed robust correlates of stimulus perception likely corresponding to the N80 and N140 components. The effect of stimulus perception was localised in the right contralateral precentral and postcentral gyri, with the left ipsilateral hemisphere contributing shortly afterwards. We found a negative relationship between the pre-stimulus alpha oscillation amplitude and stimulus perception. Moreover, greater pre-stimulus alpha phase coherence coincided with an increase in stimulus perception. There was no evidence that the alpha effects differed between stimulation modalities.

papers.title: A neuronal atlas of neurexin isoform expression in Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: The Caenorhabditis elegans neurexin gene nrx-1 encodes both long () and short ({gamma}) isoforms, but how their expression varies across individual neurons remains unclear. Using NeuroPAL and endogenous transcriptional reporters, we generated a nervous system-wide atlas of nrx-1 expression in L4 hermaphrodites. We assessed reporters for one and two {gamma} transcript groups in 267 identified neurons. The two {gamma} reporters collectively marked a broader set of neurons than the reporter, and most neurons expressing the reporter also expressed at least one {gamma} reporter. Among the ventral nerve cord motor neurons examined, reporter expression was restricted to cholinergic neurons, while one {gamma} reporter was detected exclusively in GABAergic neurons. The other {gamma} reporter was consistently detected in most cholinergic motor neurons and detected in only a subset of GABAergic motor neurons, often variably across animals. In two-fold embryos, this same {gamma} reporter was detected in more neurons than the reporter. Two upstream regulatory elements contributed to its expression in different neuronal populations. At dorsal nerve cord synapses, disruption of either isoform class reduced NRX-1 fluorescence, with a larger reduction after disruption of the short isoforms. By identifying neurons that express different combinations of long and short neurexins, this atlas provides a starting point for testing where the two isoform classes have distinct synaptic roles and where they may act together.

papers.title: A multiscale map of the descending sympathetic innervation of the spleen
papers.abstract: Brain regulation of visceral organ function depends on descending neural circuits. The spleen is the largest secondary lymphoid organ, and studies indicate that descending neural activity can alter splenic immune responses. Here, we combined retrograde tracing, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, spinal cord and brain reconstruction, and glycoprotein-complemented rabies tracing to map the sympathetic circuits associated with these organs in mice. Catecholaminergic fibers densely innervated the spleen and pancreas, and retrograde labeling identified largely distinct populations of postganglionic neurons within the celiac-superior mesenteric ganglion complex (CMG). Spleen-projecting neurons were enriched in suprarenal regions, whereas pancreas-projecting neurons were distributed more broadly. Single nucleus transcriptomics resolved three CMG neuron types and a Cre line marking the Rxfp1+ neurons labeled spleen-projecting neurons. CMG-projecting sympathetic preganglionic neurons occupied the intermediolateral cell column, intercalated nucleus, and spinal nucleus of the thoracic spinal cord. A tracing strategy designed to identify neurons upstream of these preganglionic populations labeled neurons in the medulla, pons, midbrain, hypothalamus, and several areas of the cortex including motor cortex. Motor-cortex axons formed vGlut1-positive boutons in close apposition to retrogradely labeled CMG-projecting neurons, providing anatomical support for a descending cortical route to sympathetic spinal circuits. These data provide an integrated anatomical and transcriptomic description of the descending circuits innervating the spleen and pancreas, and suggest that motor cortex is an effector cortex that controls more than movement through its projections to the spinal cord.

papers.title: Attenuated, Not Absent. Trusting Autonomous Systems Tracks Reliability More Closely, With Less Neural Engagement, Than Trusting Humans
papers.abstract: Users of autonomous systems and AI assistants decide whether to accept a system's output, yet whether such active trust decisions engage the same evaluative architecture as trust between people remains unknown. Forty-four participants made trial-by-trial decisions to trust or distrust a human or autonomous system partner during fMRI, with identical prescripted accuracy for both partners across five difficulty levels. Despite equivalent performance, trust in humans exceeded their reliability. At the highest difficulty level, the estimated probability of trusting the human partner was 72% but only 51% for the system, despite both performing at 52% accuracy. Distrust decisions recruited a prespecified performance monitoring network of valuation, salience, social-perceptual and affective regions. On hard trials, this network remained functionally coupled for both partners. Across the task, trust and distrust were discriminable in every component for both, with greater distrust-related activation and discriminability for human partners. Discriminability differences were expressed on hard trials, where partner accuracy was uncertain and trust diverged between partners. These findings indicate that trust in humans and autonomous systems engages a shared evaluative architecture, but that engagement is attenuated during autonomous system interaction. Whereas our earlier passive monitoring study found the P3a to system errors absent with no behavioural difference, an active decision appears to impose a floor of engagement, so that technology-related cognitive economization, a reduction in cognitive and social-affective resources for non-human partners, takes the form of attenuation rather than absence. Alongside this attenuation, trust in the system tracked its reliability without exceeding it.

papers.title: Subtractive and Divisive Methods for Isolating Neural Oscillations From Broadband Activity Yield Different, Even Conflicting, Power Estimates
papers.abstract: Understanding the role of oscillatory brain activity in cognition is a key objective in cognitive neuroscience. However, quantifying the power of narrowband neural oscillations is made challenging by the presence of non-oscillatory broadband activity in the signal. Recently, there has been a proliferation of methods designed to separate oscillatory from non-oscillatory (aperiodic) signals. To perform this separation, these methods must model the relationship between oscillatory and aperiodic components. Crucially, however, such methods rarely explicitly clarify whether they assume that this relationship is additive or multiplicative, an issue compounded by the common use of log-transformed data (i.e., subtraction in log space is equivalent to division in linear space). Here, we show the importance of justifying which assumption about component relations is applied. Using simulated power spectra with additive oscillatory and aperiodic components, we illustrate that methods that assume a multiplicative model, such as the popular specparam (formerly fooof) toolbox, systematically mis-estimate oscillatory activity in ways that can obscure real oscillatory differences between conditions, or even reverse their sign, creating an illusory effect. We then demonstrate these effects in two complementary empirical datasets: (a) a cross-sectional, between-subjects analysis of age-related differences in alpha power, showing how separation approaches impact effect size and detectability; and (b) a within-subjects analysis of pre-stimulus changes in alpha power in a detection task, showing how switching between approaches can greatly reduce the evidence for an effect, leading to different conclusions. These results highlight that researchers must explicitly report and justify assumptions about aperiodic and oscillatory signal combination, as these assumptions have implications not only for analyses of oscillatory activity and resultant conclusions, but also for integration of results across reports (which may implicitly employ different assumptions), and ultimately for the development of theories regarding electrophysiological features and their putative relations to cognition.

papers.title: Slow but not fast theta tACS modulation of hippocampal-cortical connectivity compresses temporal distance judgments
papers.abstract: The temporal organization of episodic memory is thought to depend critically on the hippocampus, potentially coordinated by theta-band oscillations. Here, we used concurrent transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine whether slow theta stimulation (3 Hz) applied over the left parietal cortex modulates hippocampal-cortical functional connectivity during memory encoding, and how this relates to subsequent temporal memory performance. Twenty-seven participants encoded sequences of object-scene pairs that were presented either within a single context or across a context boundary, under different tACS conditions (3 Hz, 8 Hz, and no stimulation), and afterwards judged the temporal distance between item pairs. Behaviorally, 3 Hz stimulation led to significantly compressed temporal distance judgments compared to 8 Hz, suggesting altered temporal memory reconstruction. Further, 3 Hz tACS selectively reduced hippocampal connectivity with occipital cortex, comprising left calcarine and lateral occipital clusters, and reduced hippocampal activity during encoding. In contrast, 8 Hz tACS reduced connectivity between the stimulation site and right early visual cortex. Neither frequency modulated hippocampal-cortical connectivity during retrieval. These results suggest that slow theta oscillations can shape hippocampal-cortical network dynamics in a frequency-specific manner, influencing the construction of temporal relations in memory.

papers.title: Drug Repurposing of Rapamycin Mitigates Amyloid-β-Associated Proteotoxicity in Caenorhabditis elegans Models of Alzheimer's Disease
papers.abstract: Background: Alzheimers disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia worldwide, affecting an estimated 55 million people and projected to exceed 130 million by 2050. AD is defined pathologically by extracellular accumulation of amyloid-beta (A{beta}) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles. Currently no therapy halts the underlying neurodegeneration in AD patients. Proteotoxic accumulation of A{beta} is a central pathogenic event therefore, strategies that enhance its clearance represent a compelling therapeutic avenue. Rapamycin (sirolimus), an FDA-approved allosteric inhibitor of the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) that relieves mTORC1-mediated suppression of autophagy, positioning it as an attractive drug-repurposing candidate for AD. However, it remains unclear whether rapamycins neuroprotection depends on directly reducing A{beta} burden or acts through A{beta}-independent mechanisms. This question, along with whether rapamycin alters specific A{beta} species, has not been systematically examined in a single, genetically tractable model. Methods/Results: Using two transgenic C. elegans models of human A{beta} expression a temperature-inducible, muscle-specific strain CL4176 and the pan-neuronal strain CL2355. We exposed C. elegans to 20 M rapamycin the lowest, nontoxic concentration to produce a protective effect. Rapamycin treatment delayed A{beta} induced paralysis in log-rank p = 0.0001) and improved crawling and swimming locomotion parameters. In the pan-neuronal CL2355 strain, rapamycin rescued the A{beta} induced chemotaxis deficit (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.008) without altering chemotaxis in the non-transgenic CL2122 control. Rapamycin also extended Kaplan Meier survival in CL2355 and preserved locomotor health span, delaying the trajectory of age related motor decline. At the molecular level, rapamycin did not significantly affect A{beta} burden. Conclusion: Rapamycin provides broad-spectrum and A{beta}-selective neuroprotection across muscle and neuron expressing C. elegans models of A{beta} proteotoxicity, extending from paralysis and locomotion to chemosensory behavior, longevity, and health span.

papers.title: Correlated but distinct: VIP and NDNF interneurons implement dissociable inhibitory motifs for state-dependent gain control in visual cortex
papers.abstract: VIP and NDNF positive interneurons are both found in layers 1 and 2/3 of the cortex, but have distinct patterns of gene expression, morphology, and connectivity. Despite this, their functional roles in the sensory cortices seem remarkably similar; their activity correlates with behavioral state, and they gate behaviorally driven increases in excitatory activity and sensory-driven responses. We sought to directly compare VIP and NDNF positive interneurons in the mouse visual cortex to determine if their activity was indeed functionally redundant or could be distinguished by their correlation to behavioral state, to excitatory activity, or to excitatory visual responses. Using simultaneous recordings of pupil diameter and running speed together with dual-population calcium imaging, we found that although the activity of both VIP and NDNF positive interneurons was more strongly correlated with behavior than was excitatory neuron activity, VIP positive interneuron activity was more strongly correlated with pupil diameter, whereas layer 2/3 NDNF positive interneuron activity was more strongly correlated with running speed. Excitatory-to-VIP pairwise correlation increased during locomotion, whereas excitatory-to-NDNF pairwise correlation decreased during locomotion. Intriguingly, although VIP-to-NDNF pairwise correlation was high, cortical depth significantly affected both VIP-to-NDNF correlation and the correlation of NDNF positive interneurons with pupil diameter and running speed. As expected, excitatory visual responses were significantly modulated by both pupil dilation and locomotion. However, we found that the level of VIP and NDNF activity preceding stimulus onset had a unique contribution to and was positively correlated with the amplitude of excitatory visual responses. Thus, while highly correlated to one another and to behavioral state, VIP and NDNF positive interneurons are functionally distinguishable in their relationship to both behavior and excitatory activity in the mouse visual cortex.

papers.title: Loss of metabolic resilience underlies maladaptive responses to lipid overload in TDP-43 proteinopathy
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION Altered eating behaviour is a hallmark feature of behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD). These changes may represent a compensatory response to an underlying metabolic disturbance. However, whether increased lipid availability restores metabolic homeostasis or instead accelerates disease progression remains unknown. TDP-43 proteinopathies, which account for approximately half of FTD cases, are associated with alterations in lipid metabolism, providing a mechanistic framework to investigate the cerebral response to lipid overload. METHODS We combined clinical observations in patients with bvFTD with mechanistic studies in the physiological TardbpM323K/M323K knock-in mouse model to determine how TDP-43 dysfunction modifies the response to chronic lipid excess. RESULTS In the bvFTD cohort, elevated cholesterol and triglycerides were associated with poorer cognitive performance, while mutant mice fed a lifelong high-fat diet showed worse cognitive impairment. Multi-omics analyses of the frontal cortex revealed maladaptive metabolic rewiring characterized by impaired mitochondrial and cholesterol metabolism, lipid accumulation, and widespread remodelling of TDP-43-dependent RNA processing. These alterations affected synaptic function and neuronal communication and were accompanied by reduced cerebral glucose utilization measured by 18F-FDG PET, neurotransmitter imbalance and enhanced neuroinflammation. DISCUSSION Increased lipid availability fails to compensate for TDP-43-associated metabolic dysfunction and instead promotes maladaptive molecular and functional responses. These findings identify impaired metabolic resilience as feature of TDP-43-mediated neurodegeneration and suggest that altered eating behaviour in bvFTD may represent an unsuccessful attempt to counteract an underlying metabolic deficit rather than a purely behavioural symptom. Thus, the biological context may determine whether increased energy intake is beneficial or detrimental during neurodegeneration.

papers.title: A Latent Variable Perspective on EEG Measures of Attentional Control
papers.abstract: Attentional control is a core cognitive function, yet there is still a significant debate revolving around its definition, factorial structure and underlying neural mechanisms. Research in this domain has largely developed along two largely disconnected traditions. Psychometric approaches assess individual differences using latent-variable models (e.g., structural equation modeling, confirmatory factor analysis), while cognitive neuroscience focuses on group-level behavioral and neural effects. This raises a critical question: can neural measures robust at the group level validly capture stable individual differences? Or more specifically, can some of the principles and analytical methods adopted in individual-differences research be directly applied to neural correlates of attentional control? The current study aims to address this question. Electroencephalogram data were recorded from participants as they completed four attentional control paradigms: a change detection task, the go/no-go task, the Simon task, and the Stroop task. From each task, we extracted the P3 component and a data-driven decoding accuracy measure as indices of conflict processing and tested whether these neural measures load onto a common latent factor of attentional control. Results revealed weak and largely non-significant correlations. Structural-equation modeling provided no evidence for a common latent factor, despite robust within-task effects at the group level reflected both in the behavioral and the EEG parameters. These findings suggest that EEG components may lack the construct validity needed to reliably capture individual differences in attentional control.

papers.title: Neurocognitive signatures of intrinsic motivation in naturalistic information seeking and memory
papers.abstract: Humans often seek information without direct external reward. Theories distinguish two major dimensions of this intrinsic motivation: wanting, the desire to resolve an information gap, and liking, the enjoyment of the information itself. However, how these motivational dimensions shape self-guided information-seeking behavior, neural activity, and memory formation in realworld contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, we developed a naturalistic fMRI paradigm in which participants freely browsed the internet, subsequently recalled their browsing experiences, and retrospectively reported their moment-to-moment wanting and liking. We found that both dimensions predicted more stable browsing trajectories but engaged partially dissociable neural systems: wanting recruited regions supporting goal-directed cognition, whereas liking engaged affective regions. Wanting and liking also interacted to predict memory, with wanting predicting recall primarily when liking was low. Compared with active browsing, passive viewing of the same web content reduced wanting and liking and diminished their dissociation, yet both continued to predict memory and intersubject neural similarity in the default mode network. These findings show that naturally fluctuating wanting and liking guide how we seek and remember information through overlapping yet distinct neurocognitive mechanisms.

papers.title: Confidence in global motion discrimination is better predicted by perceptual reliability than by stimulus-based heuristics
papers.abstract: Decision-making requires evaluating the reliability of perceptual estimates, but whether confidence reflects perceptual reliability or stimulus-based heuristics remains debated. We used a multiple-aperture global motion stimulus in which the global direction, and therefore motion coherence, is only available after integrating locally ambiguous signals, so that no simple stimulus statistic can serve as a shortcut. Observers reported the global direction in two successive intervals and then chose which decision was more likely to be correct. Confidence tracked accuracy beyond what coherence alone could explain: observers were more accurate in chosen intervals even at the same coherence level. Observers also frequently reported the direction opposite to the true motion, and, in direct comparisons, were more confident in these errors than in other large errors. We compared two image-computable models of motion integration. A standard motion-energy model failed to produce opposite-direction errors and the associated confidence pattern. A normalized motion-energy model, adding tuned inhibition among direction channels and an untuned gain control that increases overall activation with coherence, accounted for most of the variance in both perceptual decisions and confidence judgments. Tuned inhibition, which must be sharp if it is close to excitation in strength, produced the opposite-direction errors and reproduced the direction of their confidence advantage, and the untuned gain was needed for confidence to depend on coherence as strongly as observed. Confidence was read out from the same signal as the perceptual decision, and noise at the confidence stage, although probably present, added little to the fit beyond explaining the accuracy difference between chosen and unchosen intervals. These results suggest that confidence in this task relies on perceptual reliability. They also suggest that seemingly unusual metacognitive behavior can emerge from perceptual computations, which must therefore be modeled explicitly to identify genuine confidence mechanisms.

papers.title: Personalized functional networks scale with brain size beyond anatomy and are altered in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome
papers.abstract: Anatomically, cortical regions scale differentially with total brain size: some show disproportionate contraction in smaller brains and expansion in larger brains, while others show relative stability. Whether personalized functional networks (PFNs) follow similar areal scaling principles, and how these principles shape functional reorganization in conditions that alter brain size, remain unknown. We investigated PFN scaling in typical development (ages 8-23; n=1,332) and 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS), a neuropsychiatric genetic disorder with globally reduced brain size (62 cases, 153 matched controls; ages 10-24). In typical development, PFN scaling diverged from anatomy, deviating more from proportional scaling, particularly in association networks. In 22q11DS, accounting for expected scaling with brain size reduction revealed two robust network effects: relative peripheral visual reduction and relative cingulo-opercular enlargement. Vertex-level 22q11DS PFN reorganization beyond global cortical reduction showed spatial alignment with normative PFN changes associated with brain size, linking typical scaling principles to disorder-related alterations.

papers.title: Prediction Dynamically Modulates Gain and Width of Population Frequency Tuning in Human Auditory Cortex
papers.abstract: During perception, the brain must veridically portray sensory representations while simultaneously highlighting unexpected events. According to two-process theory of predictive perception, this balance is achieved via complementary mechanisms: precision-weighted predictions sharpen sensory tuning around expected features, while momentary surprisal scales response gain, dampening expected inputs and amplifying unexpected violations. However, standard approaches to investigate these processes, such as categorical multivariate decoding, primarily capture shifts in overall signal-to-noise, making it difficult to disentangle changes in population tuning width from modulations in response gain. Here, we combine ultra-high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (7T fMRI) with population receptive field (pRF) modelling and a continuous Bayesian ideal observer to test how expectations dynamically modulate frequency tuning across the human auditory hierarchy. We first established static pRF preferences and tuning widths independently of predictive inference. We then separately compared this static pRF tuning against two dynamically modulated alternatives. The first model evaluated how tone-by-tone precision-weighted predictions dynamically sharpen and broaden pRF tuning width, while the second model evaluated how gain (by amplification and dampening) was modulated by tone-by-tone information-theoretic surprisal. Across primary, belt, and associative auditory cortices, both a sharpening model driven by precision-weighted predictions and a gain model driven by surprisal explained significantly more variance compared to a static baseline model. Counterfactual models inverting these driving features yielded no improvement, ruling out non-specific model mimicry. Additionally, contrasting local and global tonotopic implementations revealed a feature-selective dissociation: whereas precision-weighted predictions locally sharpened pRFs tuned to expected frequencies, surprisal acted as a global broadcast signal that multiplicatively scaled pRF gain across all frequency channels of the tonotopic map. Together, these findings demonstrate that the auditory system continuously balances selectivity for expected structure and responsiveness to surprising input through local sharpening and global gain modulation.

papers.title: Waveform morphology links local circuit kinetics to cortical interactions
papers.abstract: How does local cortical physiology shape interactions between brain regions? We combined neural mass modelling with human and macaque intracranial recordings to examine how synaptic kinetics link oscillatory waveform morphology to cortical interactions. In a modified excitatory-inhibitory Wilson-Cowan model, synaptic rise and decay kinetics shaped waveform geometry and phase-dependent responsiveness. Local kinetics and coupling symmetry jointly influenced interaction measures and temporal irreversibility, while phase-locked perturbations altered imaginary coherency and bivariate irreversibility even when the coupling strengths remained fixed. In stereo-EEG from 23 patients, waveform asymmetry was most strongly associated with local irreversibility, whereas mean instantaneous alpha frequency showed stronger associations with interregional measures. Subdural macaque electrocorticography reproduced the frequency associations but not the local waveform association. Together, these findings show that waveform shape carries information about local neuronal dynamics, provide a mechanistic framework for interpreting cortical interactions, and motivate testing waveform morphology as a guide to stimulation timing.

papers.title: Age-dependent changes in the putamen transcriptome and proteome of a transgenic minipig model of Huntington's disease
papers.abstract: Huntington's disease is an inherited neurodegenerative disorder with no disease-modifying treatment available. Preclinical trials of gene therapies rely on large animal models and the transgenic Huntington's disease (TgHD) minipig is one of them. Minipigs live more than a decade, so the effect of a single dose of gene therapy can be followed for years. The TgHD transgene carries a mixed CAG/CAA repeat that is not expected to expand somatically. However, its putamen, part of the striatum that degenerates first in patients, had not been examined by genome-wide methods, nor beyond 4 years of age. We compared the putamen of transgenic and wild-type minipigs at 4 and 8 years by RNA sequencing and label-free mass spectrometry proteomics, and measured mutant huntingtin by immunoassay. Seven genes were differentially expressed at 4 years and 3,324 at 8 years, and the pathway changes of the transcriptome and the proteome were concordant at that age. The D2 medium spiny neuron marker gene set was reduced at 8 years in both the transcriptome and the proteome. Mitochondrial and oxidative phosphorylation pathways were positively enriched at 4 years and negatively enriched at 8 years. Immune and complement pathways were positively enriched at 8 years, and the number of altered splicing events increased almost fivefold between 4 and 8 years. We detected no age-dependent accumulation of soluble mutant huntingtin. Since the repeat does not expand, these changes developed without somatic expansion, a major driver of progression in human Huntington's disease. We propose that the reduced neuronal markers reflect a loss of neuronal identity rather than neuronal death. The TgHD minipig would then recapitulate the slow early phase of the disease, when treatment is arguably most likely to help.

papers.title: An isogenic human stem cell model reveals NGLY1-dependent control of microglial development
papers.abstract: NGLY1 is a cytosolic N-glycanase involved in glycoprotein quality control and proteasome-mediated protein degradation and is critical for normal brain development and function. Although neuronal alterations caused by NGLY1 deficiency have been extensively characterized in animal and human cell models, how NGLY1 deficiency affects human glial cells, particularly microglia, the brain-resident innate immune cells, remains largely unknown. Using patient-derived NGLY1-deficient human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) lines and their corresponding CRISPR-mediated gene-corrected isogenic lines, we found that NGLY1-deficient primitive macrophage progenitors (PMPs) exhibited increased GlcNAc-Asn (GNA) accumulation and elevated expression of RUNX1, a key transcription factor regulating myeloid lineage development, accompanied by abnormal proliferation. Following further differentiation, NGLY1-deficient human microglia exhibited reduced morphological complexity and impaired phagocytic capacity. In addition, NGLY1-deficient microglia showed increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-1{beta}, IL-6, and TNF, under both basal and stimulated conditions, indicative of a heightened inflammatory state. Mechanistically, our data showed that RUNX1 upregulation induced by NGLY1 deficiency partially mediated impaired PMP proliferation and subsequent microglial abnormalities, implicating RUNX1 dysregulation in NGLY1-associated microglial dysfunction and identifying RUNX1 as a potential therapeutic target. Together, using patient-derived and gene-corrected isogenic hiPSCs, our study establishes a human stem cell platform for modeling NGLY1 deficiency and reveals that impaired deglycosylation alters human microglial developmental trajectories and ultimately compromises microglial homeostasis and function. These microglial abnormalities may contribute to the neurological deficits observed in patients carrying loss-of-function variants in NGLY1.

papers.title: A four-dimensional single-cell and spatial atlas of cAMP-driven repair after rat spinal cord injury
papers.abstract: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) induction through photoactivatable adenylate cyclase (bPAC) in corticospinal neurons enhances locomotion after spinal cord injury (SCI); however, the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie this improvement are unknown. Here we perform single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST) of spinal cord sections at the injury site of dorsal hemisected rats, to identify the pathways through which bPAC stimulation exerts its regenerative cues after SCI, along with the changes in cellular populations that occur in different parts of the spinal cord.
